question: State what is meant by retained profit as a source of business finance.

points: Profit that has been kept / reinvested in the business rather than distributed to owners/shareholders (1)

topic: D1 Internal finance — sale of assets
question: Give two examples of internal sources of finance for a business.

points: Retained profit (1)
Sale of assets (1)
Owner's personal savings / owner's capital (1)
Reducing stock / working capital (1)

question: State two features of a bank overdraft.

points: Short-term borrowing facility allowing the business to spend beyond its current account balance (1)
Interest is charged daily on the overdrawn amount (1)
Repayable on demand by the bank (1)
Usually requires an agreed limit set by the bank (1)

question: Identify two features of trade credit.

points: Supplier allows the business to receive goods now and pay later (1)
Typically 30–90 days credit period (1)
No interest charged if paid within the agreed terms (1)
Effectively a short-term, interest-free source of finance (1)

question: State two features of hire purchase (HP).

points: Business makes fixed regular payments over an agreed period (1)
Asset is owned by the finance company until the final payment is made (1)
Interest is charged on the HP agreement (1)
Business can use the asset during the payment period (1)

question: Give two differences between leasing and hire purchase.

points: Leasing: the business never owns the asset; HP: ownership transfers at the end (1)
Leasing: maintenance may be included; HP: the business is responsible for maintenance once it has the asset (1)
Leasing: usually lower monthly cost; HP: business building equity in the asset (1)

question: State two features of raising finance through a share issue.

points: No interest to repay (unlike a loan) (1)
New shareholders become part-owners of the business (1)
Does not have to be repaid (1)
Only available to limited companies (1)

question: Identify two features of debentures (bonds) as a source of business finance.

points: Long-term loan notes issued by a company to investors (1)
Carry a fixed interest rate (coupon) paid to holders (1)
Repaid on a set maturity date (1)
Typically available only to large limited companies (1)

question: Give two advantages of grants as a source of finance for a business.

points: Does not have to be repaid (1)
No interest charged (1)
Improves cash flow without increasing debt (1)

question: State two features of crowdfunding as a source of business finance.

points: Raises small amounts from large numbers of people via an online platform (1)
Can be equity-based (investors receive shares) or reward-based (backers receive a product/perk) (1)
The business retains control if using reward-based rather than equity crowdfunding (1)
Success is not guaranteed — the campaign may not reach its target (1)

question: Identify two features of venture capital as a source of business finance.

points: Provided by specialist investors (VCs) to high-growth, high-risk businesses (1)
VC firm usually takes an equity stake in the business (1)
Investors may offer business expertise and contacts as well as finance (1)
Typically involves giving up some ownership and control (1)

question: Give two features of a bank loan as a source of business finance.

points: Fixed or variable interest charged on the amount borrowed (1)
Repaid over an agreed period in regular instalments (1)
May require security / collateral (1)
Loan amount is agreed upfront and drawn down in full (1)

question: State two differences between internal and external sources of finance.

points: Internal sources come from within the business; external sources come from outside the business (1)
Internal sources do not require repayment with interest; external sources usually involve repayment or giving up ownership (1)
Internal sources are often limited in scale; external sources can raise larger amounts (1)

question: Identify two sources of short-term external finance for a business.

points: Bank overdraft (1)
Trade credit (1)
Short-term bank loan (1)
Invoice factoring / debtor finance (1)

question: Give two sources of long-term external finance for a business.

points: Share issue (1)
Debentures / bonds (1)
Long-term bank loan (1)
Venture capital (1)
Mortgage (1)

topic: D2 External finance — overdraft vs loan
scenario: TechFix Ltd needs £2,000 to cover an unexpected repair bill that is due this month but expects to receive a large client payment next month.
question: Explain why a bank overdraft would be more suitable than a bank loan for TechFix Ltd in this situation.

points: An overdraft is a short-term facility that can be used and repaid quickly (1) which suits TechFix's needs as it only needs the money for a short period until the client payment arrives next month (1)
A bank loan would involve longer-term repayments with more interest charges (1) making it more expensive than an overdraft for a short-term cash flow need (1)

scenario: A bakery wants to acquire a new industrial oven costing £12,000 but does not have enough cash.
question: Explain one advantage to the bakery of using hire purchase to buy the oven.

points: The bakery does not need to pay the full £12,000 upfront (1) so it can preserve its cash for other operating costs while still using the oven to generate revenue (1)
The oven becomes an owned asset at the end of the HP agreement (1) which the bakery can then use as security for future borrowing or sell if needed (1)

scenario: UrbanStyle Ltd is a fast-growing clothing retailer considering two options to finance a £500,000 expansion: a bank loan at 7% interest or a new share issue.
question: Explain two advantages to UrbanStyle Ltd of using a share issue rather than a bank loan.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each advantage. Maximum 4 marks.
points: A share issue does not require interest payments (1) whereas a bank loan at 7% would add significant interest costs to UrbanStyle's expenses, reducing profit (1)
Share capital does not have to be repaid (1) reducing UrbanStyle's financial obligations if trading is difficult, unlike a loan that must be serviced monthly (1)
New shareholders may bring expertise or contacts (1) as well as funding, benefiting the business beyond finance (1)

topic: D2 External finance — share issue vs loan
scenario: UrbanStyle Ltd is a fast-growing clothing retailer considering two options to finance a £500,000 expansion: a bank loan at 7% interest or a new share issue.
question: Explain two disadvantages to UrbanStyle Ltd of using a share issue.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each disadvantage. Maximum 4 marks.
points: New shareholders become part-owners and may want a say in how the business is run (1) which dilutes the control of the existing owners (1)
Dividends may need to be paid to shareholders (1) which is an ongoing cost, unlike the interest on a bank loan which ends when the loan is repaid (1)
Issuing shares is complex and costly — legal and administrative costs apply (1) particularly for a public share issue (1)

scenario: GreenGrocer Ltd has been trading for five years and has £80,000 of retained profit available. It is planning a £50,000 refurbishment of its main store.
question: Explain two advantages to GreenGrocer Ltd of using retained profit to fund the refurbishment.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each advantage. Maximum 4 marks.
points: No interest is payable (1) unlike a bank loan, so the full benefit of the investment goes to the business (1)
The business does not need to give up any ownership or control (1) as no new shareholders or lenders are involved (1)
There is no repayment obligation (1) which protects GreenGrocer's cash flow if trading is slower than expected after the refurbishment (1)

scenario: TechStartup Ltd has developed a new AI-powered app and needs £500,000 to scale. It is considering venture capital investment.
question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to TechStartup Ltd of accepting venture capital.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for advantage and 1+1 for disadvantage.
points: Advantage: The VC firm brings industry expertise and a network of contacts (1) which could help TechStartup Ltd grow more quickly beyond just providing the £500,000 funding (1)
Disadvantage: The VC firm will require an equity stake in TechStartup (1) meaning the founders give up a portion of ownership and may have less control over strategic decisions (1)

scenario: SocialEats is a new restaurant business looking to raise £30,000 through a reward-based crowdfunding campaign.
question: Explain two advantages to SocialEats of using reward-based crowdfunding rather than a bank loan.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each advantage. Maximum 4 marks.
points: No interest or repayment is required on reward-based crowdfunding (1) unlike a bank loan which would add to SocialEats' monthly costs (1)
A successful crowdfunding campaign markets the restaurant to potential customers (1) building awareness and a loyal customer base before the business even opens (1)
No security / collateral is needed (1) unlike a bank loan which may require assets as security (1)

scenario: Rapid Deliveries Ltd is considering whether to buy a new fleet of vans using a bank loan or lease them from a finance company.
question: Explain two advantages to Rapid Deliveries Ltd of leasing the vans instead of buying them.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each advantage. Maximum 4 marks.
points: Leasing preserves cash and avoids a large capital outlay (1) leaving more working capital available for day-to-day operations (1)
The lessor often handles maintenance (1) reducing unexpected repair costs and administration for Rapid Deliveries (1)
Vans can be upgraded at the end of the lease (1) ensuring the fleet is always modern and fuel-efficient without a large reinvestment (1)

scenario: BuildRight Ltd is a small construction firm that regularly purchases materials from suppliers on 60-day trade credit terms.
question: Explain how trade credit benefits BuildRight Ltd's cash flow.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each point. Maximum 4 marks.
points: Trade credit allows BuildRight to use the materials for 60 days before paying for them (1) which means it can potentially complete work and receive payment from clients before it needs to pay its suppliers (1)
This effectively provides 60 days of interest-free short-term financing (1) improving the firm's working capital position without any cost (1)

scenario: EcoSolar is a small business installing solar panels. It has been awarded a £25,000 government grant to support its expansion into rural areas.
question: Explain two advantages to EcoSolar of using a grant rather than a bank loan to fund this expansion.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each advantage. Maximum 4 marks.
points: The grant does not have to be repaid (1) so EcoSolar can expand without accumulating debt (1)
No interest is charged (1) meaning the full £25,000 goes into the project rather than partly servicing debt (1)
The grant does not dilute ownership (1) unlike issuing shares to raise the funds (1)

scenario: PrimePrint Ltd is taking out a £40,000 5-year bank loan to buy new printing machinery.
question: Explain one disadvantage to PrimePrint Ltd of using a bank loan for this purpose.

points: The loan attracts interest charges over 5 years (1) increasing the total cost of the machinery beyond the original £40,000 and reducing PrimePrint's profit (1)
If PrimePrint's revenue falls, it still has to make fixed monthly repayments (1) which could put the business under financial strain (1)

scenario: GlobalPort PLC needs to raise £10 million for a new deep-water terminal. It is considering issuing debentures rather than approaching a bank.
question: Explain two advantages to GlobalPort PLC of issuing debentures rather than taking a bank loan.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each advantage. Maximum 4 marks.
points: Debentures can raise large sums from multiple investors simultaneously (1) which may be more practical for £10 million than a single bank loan from one lender (1)
Interest on debentures is a fixed, predictable cost (1) making long-term financial planning easier for GlobalPort (1)
The interest rate on debentures may be lower than a bank loan because investors compete to buy them (1) reducing GlobalPort's financing costs (1)

topic: D1/D2 Sources of finance — choice factors
question: Explain two factors a business should consider when choosing between internal and external sources of finance.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each factor. Maximum 4 marks.
points: The amount needed — internal sources may be insufficient for large investments (1) so external sources may be necessary when the business lacks sufficient retained profit or assets to sell (1)
The impact on control — external sources such as share issues dilute ownership (1) whereas internal sources keep full control with existing owners (1)
Cost — interest and fees on external finance add to costs (1) whereas internal sources avoid these charges (1)

scenario: SunBake Ltd is a start-up bakery with no trading history. It is struggling to secure a bank loan.
question: Explain two alternative external sources of finance SunBake Ltd could consider.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each source. Maximum 4 marks.
points: Crowdfunding (reward-based) — SunBake could raise money from customers by offering them free products or early access (1) without needing security or a trading history (1)
Venture capital — if the business model is sufficiently scalable, a VC firm may invest (1) in exchange for an equity stake (1)
Government / small business grants — as a food business in an enterprise zone, it may qualify for grants (1) which do not need repayment (1)

scenario: RetailRush Ltd has a seasonal business with high sales in December but very low sales in January–February.
question: Explain why a bank overdraft is a suitable source of finance for RetailRush during January and February.

points: An overdraft is flexible and can be drawn on and repaid as needed (1) so RetailRush can use it to cover outgoings in January and repay it quickly once sales pick up later in the year (1)

scenario: GrowFast Ltd is a profitable private limited company that has been trading for eight years. It wants to invest £200,000 to open a second branch. It has £100,000 in retained profit available.
question: Discuss which source or combination of sources of finance GrowFast Ltd should use to fund its expansion. (6)

indicative_content: Retained profit: £100,000 available — free, no dilution, but only covers half the cost
Bank loan for remaining £100,000: predictable repayments, maintains ownership, requires interest
Share issue: raises more capital but dilutes control — already a private company so limited share market
Could use HP or leasing if any of the £200,000 is for equipment
Overdraft: not suitable for large long-term investment
Balanced approach: use retained profit (£100k) to minimise external borrowing, plus bank loan for remaining £100k
Conclusion must be justified with reference to the scenario numbers and GrowFast's situation

level_descriptors.descriptor: Identifies one source; little analysis or application to the scenario.
Considers two or more sources; begins to weigh advantages/disadvantages; partial conclusion.
Well-developed, balanced discussion; recommends a combination with justification; considers cost, control and risk; supported conclusion.

topic: D2 External finance — crowdfunding vs loan
scenario: Luna is launching a sustainable clothing brand. She needs £40,000. She is considering a 3-year bank loan at 9.5% APR or an equity crowdfunding campaign offering 20% of the business.
question: Discuss which option Luna should choose to finance her new business. (6)

indicative_content: Bank loan: predictable monthly repayments; maintains full ownership; 9.5% interest adds to costs; requires credit history / collateral — may be harder as a start-up
Equity crowdfunding: no repayments or interest; builds community of investors; 20% ownership lost permanently; investors may interfere in decisions
Luna is a start-up with no trading history — bank may refuse the loan
If crowdfunding is successful, she gets marketing exposure alongside finance
Long-term: 20% equity could be very costly if business grows significantly
Conclusion: if loan is available, it preserves ownership; if not accessible, crowdfunding is viable alternative; depends on Luna's growth ambitions

level_descriptors.descriptor: Describes one option; little comparison.
Compares both options; considers cost and ownership implications; partial conclusion.
Well-developed, balanced discussion; considers start-up viability, cost of debt vs equity, long-term ownership; justified conclusion.

topic: D2 External finance — VC vs bank loan
scenario: RapidTech is a three-year-old tech business turning over £800,000. It needs £1.2m to develop its next product. Options: a bank loan at 8% over 5 years, or venture capital from TechFund who would take a 35% stake.
question: Discuss whether RapidTech should accept venture capital or take the bank loan. (6)

indicative_content: VC: no interest or repayment; TechFund brings expertise and network; 35% equity given away permanently
Bank loan: retains 100% ownership; fixed interest cost at 8% over 5 years; requires regular repayments from revenue
RapidTech turnover £800k — monthly loan repayments on £1.2m at 8% over 5 years would be significant
VC money may allow faster growth, making the 35% stake worthwhile in absolute terms
If RapidTech founders want to exit via sale later, VC support could increase valuation
Risk: VC may push for faster growth or early exit that conflicts with founder's vision
Balanced conclusion: depends on founders' priorities (control vs growth speed)

level_descriptors.descriptor: Describes one option; minimal analysis.
Compares both; considers ownership and cost; partial conclusion.
Well-developed comparison; uses revenue data; considers cost, control, expertise, long-term implications; justified conclusion.

scenario: PrintMasters Ltd needs to replace its printing press (cost £80,000). Options: buy outright using retained profit of £80,000; HP over 3 years at 11% APR; or an operating lease at £1,800 per month.
question: Discuss which option PrintMasters Ltd should choose to finance the new press. (6)

indicative_content: Buy outright: no interest, full ownership immediately; but uses all retained profit — no cash buffer
HP: retains cash; interest cost 11% APR; owns asset after 3 years; monthly payments manageable
Lease: lowest monthly cost initially; never owns the asset; ongoing long-term cost; flexibility to upgrade
If retained profit is their only cash buffer, using it all is risky
HP total cost = £80,000 + interest — more expensive than buying outright
Lease: total over 3 years = £1,800 x 36 = £64,800 but never owns the press
Conclusion: HP probably best balance — preserves cash while building ownership; outright purchase cheapest but risky if it depletes all reserves

level_descriptors.descriptor: Describes one option; no quantification or comparison.
Compares two or more options; some financial analysis; partial conclusion.
Thorough comparison of all three with costs considered; relates to PrintMasters' cash position; justified conclusion.

topic: D2 External finance — grants and trade credit
scenario: NewHarvest is a small organic farm business. It has been offered a £15,000 government grant for renewable energy equipment. It currently uses 30-day trade credit with its suppliers and is considering extending to 60 days.
question: Discuss two sources of finance that NewHarvest is using or could use to improve its financial position. (6)

indicative_content: Government grant: no repayment — ideal for the renewable energy investment; may come with conditions on how money is spent; strengthens cash position
Trade credit extension 30→60 days: provides an additional 30 days interest-free working capital; depends on supplier agreement; could strain supplier relationships
Combining grant with 60-day credit could significantly improve cash flow
Grants are competitive and may not cover full cost of equipment
Over-reliance on supplier goodwill is a risk
Conclusion: grant is highly beneficial; trade credit extension is a low-cost option but requires negotiation and good supplier relations

level_descriptors.descriptor: Briefly describes one source; minimal analysis.
Discusses both sources with some analysis of benefits and risks.
Well-developed discussion of both sources in context; considers conditions and risks; justified conclusion.

scenario: StarBite Ltd is a chain of 12 sandwich shops with annual turnover of £1.8m and net profit of £120,000. It wants to open 6 new shops in 18 months. Each new shop costs £85,000 to set up. It has £60,000 retained profit and no existing long-term debt. [Table: Bank loan — 8.5% APR over 5 years available up to £400k; Share issue — 10 new investors offering £35,000 each for 3% each; Franchise investment model — franchisees fund set-up, StarBite earns 8% royalty; Government Start Up loan — 6% fixed rate up to £25,000 per director, max 2 directors]
question: Evaluate which sources of finance StarBite Ltd should use to fund its expansion. (12)

indicative_content: Total needed: 6 x £85,000 = £510,000; retained profit covers only £60,000
Bank loan up to £400k: 8.5% interest; total ≈ £510k needed; combined with retained profit £60k + bank loan up to £400k = £460k — still £50k short
Share issue: 10 x £35k = £350k available; gives away 30% of the business; dilutes control significantly
Start-up loans: 2 directors x £25k = £50k at 6%; useful top-up for shortfall
Franchise model: no capital required from StarBite; royalty income ongoing; loses some control over brand; rapid expansion possible
Combination: franchise model for some shops + retained profit for controlled investment with minimal debt
Best strategy likely: franchise 4 shops (no capital) + open 2 using retained profit + £25k Start-Up loans = £60k + £50k = £110k enough for 1 shop, franchise covers the rest
Alternative: bank loan + retained profit for 6 shops but 8.5% adds £34k+ annually to costs
Conclusion: franchise model is most financially efficient; combined approach with Start-Up loans and retained profit for 1-2 directly owned shops is sound

level_descriptors.descriptor: Identifies one or two sources; little or no quantification; basic conclusion.
Considers multiple sources; uses some figures; addresses control or cost implications; partial conclusion.
Balanced evaluation of at least three sources; quantifies needs and costs; considers control and risk; supported conclusion.

Thorough, well-developed evaluation; uses all key data; considers cost of debt, dilution, franchise model benefits and risks; develops a clear, justified strategy; specialist vocabulary throughout; acknowledges trade-offs.

scenario: CraftBrew PLC is a listed craft beer company with turnover £5m. It needs £2m to build a new brewing facility. It is considering: A) A rights issue (existing shareholders offered new shares at a discount); B) Issuing £2m of 5-year debentures at 5% annual interest; C) A sale-and-leaseback of its current headquarters (valued at £3m). [Table: Annual profit £280,000; Existing gearing ratio 30%; Interest cover ratio 4x; Shareholder dividend yield: 3.2%]
question: Evaluate which option CraftBrew PLC should use to raise the £2m. (12)

indicative_content: Rights issue: no interest or repayment; dilutes EPS and dividends if profit unchanged; existing shareholders offered shares at discount — may be accepted or not
Debentures at 5%: £2m x 5% = £100k annual interest; interest cover 4x on £280k profit means interest payments manageable (£280k/£100k = 2.8x cover — acceptable but reduced)
Gearing: currently 30%; adding £2m debt may push gearing high depending on total equity — potential concern for lenders
Sale-and-leaseback: raises £3m+ from HQ sale; must then pay rent forever; loses ownership of strategic asset; improves cash but increases long-term costs
Rights issue preserves lower gearing; debentures add to gearing but maintain full ownership for current shareholders
Sale-and-leaseback: generates more than needed but loses an asset; ongoing lease cost reduces future profit
Conclusion: debentures are likely most appropriate — fixed, known cost; interest cover manageable; preserves ownership without permanent equity dilution; gearing impact manageable

level_descriptors.descriptor: Describes one option; limited use of financial data; basic conclusion.
Compares two or more options; uses some ratio/data; partial evaluation.
Balanced evaluation of all three; uses gearing, interest cover, and cost data; supported conclusion.
Thorough evaluation; uses all ratios and data; considers long-term cost, gearing, ownership, shareholder impact; specialist vocabulary; well-justified conclusion.

scenario: Paulo has designed a new smart home device. He needs £120,000 to manufacture the first batch and launch marketing. He has £20,000 personal savings and no assets to offer as security. He has a strong business plan but no trading history. Options: A) Personal bank loan up to £25,000 at 12% APR; B) Equity crowdfunding — offer 25% stake; C) Government-backed Start Up Loan (6%, £25k max per director, Paulo is sole director); D) Angel investor — £100,000 for 40% equity and a board seat. [Table: Projected Year 1 revenue £200,000; Projected Year 1 profit £35,000; Market size estimated £50m; Cost per unit £60; Selling price £140]
question: Evaluate which combination of finance sources Paulo should use to fund his launch. (12)

indicative_content: Total needed: £120,000; personal savings: £20,000 — leaves £100,000 gap
Personal bank loan: £25,000 max + Start Up Loan £25k = £50k external borrowing at reasonable rates; combined with savings = £70k — still £50k short
Equity crowdfunding 25%: if campaign raises needed amount, gives away 25% permanently; builds customer base; no repayments
Angel investor: £100k covers 83% of gap; 40% equity + board seat — significant loss of control; Year 1 profit £35k split 60/40
Combination approach: personal savings £20k + Start Up Loan £25k = £45k; angel investor for remaining £75k (re-negotiate lower stake?); avoids costly bank loan interest
Alternatively: savings + Start Up Loan + crowdfunding — retains more control than angel; lower certainty
No collateral: bank loan beyond Start Up Loan likely inaccessible
Angel brings expertise and network in smart home sector — strategic value
Conclusion: angel investor or crowdfunding + Start Up Loan; angel preferred if Paulo accepts reduced control in exchange for expertise; Start Up Loan as top-up in all scenarios

level_descriptors.descriptor: Identifies one or two sources; little use of data; basic conclusion.
Considers multiple sources; uses some financial projections; partial analysis of control and cost.
Balanced evaluation of all four sources; quantifies funding gap; considers control, cost, expertise; supported conclusion.

Thorough evaluation; uses all data including projections, cost per unit and market size; constructs optimal combination strategy; considers long-term ownership impact; specialist vocabulary; clear, justified conclusion with trade-offs.
